newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Index volume slow, volatility off.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Index volume slow, volatility off.

text.p: U.S. stock index options volume remained relatively thin Wednesday and volatilities continued to ease as players digested Tuesday's reaction to news that the Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged.
In major index options trading, put volume continued to outpace call volume, giving the contrarian bulls another reason to think the market would work its way higher.
By 1130 CDT/1630 GMT, S&P 100 index .OEX puts outpaced calls by 26,563 to 21,099 and S&P 500 index .SPX puts led calls by 20,537 to 11,568.
Jerry Hegarty, an analyst at Thomson Financial Services, said in a report that in the first two days of the June expiration cycle, OEX put volume outpaced call volume by about 100,000 contracts.
But he noted that the numbers could be somewhat misleading because volumes have been so thin.

"Monday was the lowest volume day for the market this year, and that also translated into lower options volume for the OEX," said Joseph Sunderman, an analyst at Investment Research Institute in Cincinnati.
He called the recent 1.8 OEX put/call ratio reading "off the charts" relative to historic levels, but added, "I'd rather see it on higher volume."
Sunderman said that while the market could see a further pullback over the next few sessions, he expected it to move higher in the near term.
In early afternoon trading Wednesday, the Dow industrial average .DJI was down about 58 points at 7,245 and the SPX was off 5.46 at 836.20. The OEX fell 5.29 to 823.03.
Despite the drop, index options volatilities continued to ease after spiking higher last Friday and Monday.
The Chicago Board Options Exchange's volatility index .VIX was down 0.28 at 21.42. The index is calculated off certain OEX options.

"We definitely think things are going to cool down a little bit becuase they've moved up so hard," said Bill Yates at DYR Associates. "But on the other hand, we don't see any reason for it to go down."
He said that within the market, volatilities in general are easing, with most stock groups well into overbought territory.

"We look for stocks that drop down and we can sell some options against them because implied volatilities have gotten higher," Yates explained. "But we're not finding any stocks that are good fundamental value for establishing buy-writes on."
He said that as stock prices have moved higher, premiums decline as volatilities on the options decline.

"We're not finding many stocks that have been taken out and shot, so we can't get any volatility that's worth selling options on," he said. "If you're going to do something right now, with low volatility, you could look to buy some options."
